copy.title: The ferry
copy.body: Seattle to Bainbridge is about a 35-minute crossing. Jumbo Mark II ferries such as the Tacoma, Wenatchee and Puyallup serve the route. Leaving the dock, a ferry sounds one prolonged blast, as the inland rules require.

a11y.label: The ferry, island story
a11y.announce: The ferry. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Port Blakely mill
copy.body: Captain William Renton's mill opened in 1864. By 1882 it was the largest on the Pacific Coast. It burned in 1888 and 1907 and closed in the early 1920s (sources say 1922 or 1923). Today a few pilings, a crumbling concrete building and a mill pond remain.

a11y.label: Port Blakely mill, island story
a11y.announce: Port Blakely mill. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Nidoto Nai Yoni
copy.body: On March 30, 1942, 227 Japanese American islanders were forced from their homes and sent from the Eagledale ferry dock, the first removal under Executive Order 9066. The memorial wall names all 276 islanders of Japanese descent who were excluded. Its words, Nidoto Nai Yoni, mean: Let it not happen again.

a11y.label: Remembrance
a11y.announce: Remembrance: the Japanese American Exclusion Memorial.

copy.title: Yama
copy.body: Japanese immigrant families who worked at the Port Blakely mill lived in a village called Yama, on mill land above the harbor. The site is on the National Register and is protected, so it is not shown on the map.

a11y.label: Yama, island story
a11y.announce: Yama, a village above Blakely Harbor.

copy.title: Battle Point helix house
copy.body: From the early 1940s this was a Navy radio transmitting station, with an 800 ft tower beside the helix house, which matched transmitters to antennas. It closed in 1959. Volunteers saved the helix house in 1992 and built an observatory on it, now the Battle Point Observatory (renamed in June 2025).

a11y.label: Battle Point helix house, island story
a11y.announce: Battle Point helix house. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Fort Ward batteries
copy.body: A coast-artillery post from 1903. Batteries Thornburgh and Vinton held 3-inch guns until 1920; two other batteries stand on private land and are not mapped. From 1939 the Navy's Station S listening post intercepted Japanese naval radio here. The Army fort closed in 1928, the Navy left in 1958, and the park passed to the park district in 2011.

a11y.label: Fort Ward batteries, island story
a11y.announce: Fort Ward batteries. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Eagle Harbor and Winslow
copy.body: The Hall Brothers shipyard moved here from Port Blakely in 1902 and 1903. The town of Madrone became Winslow, after Winslow Hall.

a11y.label: Eagle Harbor and Winslow, island story
a11y.announce: Eagle Harbor and Winslow. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Strawberry fields
copy.body: Japanese American families were known for Bainbridge strawberries. Filipino immigrants came from the late 1920s to work the farms, and during the war many Japanese American farmers left their farms in the care of Filipino American farmhands. The community hall near Strawberry Hill was built in 1928; the Strawberry Festival dates to 1948 (one source says 1950).

a11y.label: Strawberry fields, island story
a11y.announce: Strawberry fields. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Fort Ward's quiet guns
copy.body: Fort Ward was an Army coast-artillery post from 1903 to 1928. Its guns were removed in 1920 and never fired in anger. The Navy took over in 1938 and left in 1958; the land was a state park from 1960 to 2011, then passed to the park district.

a11y.label: Fort Ward's quiet guns, island story
a11y.announce: Fort Ward's quiet guns. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Hall Brothers' shipyard
copy.body: Beside the Port Blakely mill, the Hall Brothers' yard launched 77 ships between 1881 and 1904. Down on the shore, the skeleton of a generator building still stands.

a11y.label: Hall Brothers' shipyard, island story
a11y.announce: Hall Brothers' shipyard. 15 marks when you finish.

copy.title: Moritani Preserve
copy.body: Hyakutaro Moritani came from Hiroshima in 1905 and planted Marshall strawberries here. Sent away in 1942, the family came back after the war and farmed until the 1960s. Only the porch steps remain. The Fletcher Bay Foundation kept the 8.5 acres as a preserve around 2017.

a11y.label: Moritani Preserve, island story
a11y.announce: Moritani Preserve, an island story.

copy.title: Battle Point
copy.body: About 90 acres here were cleared in 1941 for a Navy radio transmitter site. It was deactivated in 1959 and passed to the park district in 1972. The concrete Helix House, once slated for demolition, is now the Battle Point Observatory, built by volunteers and renamed in June 2025.

a11y.label: Battle Point, island story
a11y.announce: Battle Point. 15 marks when you finish.
